```{r setup}
#| include: false
# Figures come from scripts/90_report_figs.R (figs/<figure>_<profile>.png + manifest.csv).
# The CONUS ("full") version of a figure is shown when it exists, otherwise the dev one.
figs <- if (file.exists("figs/manifest.csv")) {
  utils::read.csv("figs/manifest.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
} else data.frame(figure = character(), profile = character())

show_fig <- function(name, caption, alt = caption) {
  m <- figs[figs$figure == name, , drop = FALSE]
  pick <- intersect(c("full", "dev"), m$profile)
  pick <- pick[file.exists(sprintf("figs/%s_%s.png", name, pick))]
  if (!length(pick)) {
    cat(sprintf('\n::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}\n## Figure pending\n%s\n:::\n\n',
                caption))
    return(invisible())
  }
  r <- m[m$profile == pick[1], ][1, ]
  note <- sprintf("[%s · %s · figure made %s]{.fig-meta}", r$extent, r$years, r$made)
  cat(sprintf('\n![%s %s](figs/%s_%s.png){#fig-%s fig-alt="%s" .column-page-right}\n\n',
              caption, note, name, pick[1], gsub("_", "-", name), alt))
}
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Work in progress
This page tracks an ongoing analysis and is updated as the work moves along. Results
shown here are **preliminary** and some come from a small Arizona test area. They are
here to show the approach and invite feedback, not for operational use. The
[changelog](#changelog) lists what changed and when.
:::

## At a glance

**The question.** Where across the contiguous U.S. do herbaceous fuels (grasses and
forbs) share a common seasonal pattern of green-up, staying green and curing? Regions
like that are the domains we need to build and tune **regional phenology models**
for live fuel moisture, instead of applying one set of thresholds everywhere.

**The approach.** Two independent ways of drawing regions, then compare them:

- **Cut A, climate:** cluster grid cells on climate descriptors built from daily PRISM
  data. These regions are *hypotheses about what drives* fuel phenology.
- **Cut B, satellite curves:** cluster grid cells on the observed seasonal curves of
  greenness and canopy water from MODIS. This is the *response* and the real test of
  Cut A.
- **Ground observations** from the USA National Phenology Network (NPN) and
  iNaturalist provide an independent check, including in places where satellite
  curves and land-cover maps are hardest to interpret.

Where the climate and satellite regions agree, there is a solid basis for regional
models. Where they disagree is where to look for what's missing.

**Status (October 2026).**

| Component | Status |
|---|---|
| Daily PRISM climate, 4 km, CONUS, 2001–2025 | Done |
| Grid, elevation and herbaceous cover layers (Annual NLCD) | Done |
| MODIS greenness and canopy water, CONUS, 2001–2025 | Done (Terra and Aqua merged, smoothed daily curves per year) |
| Cut A, Block 1: seasonal climate features | Done (CONUS, water years 2002–2025) |
| Cut A, Block 2: timing and variability features | Done (CONUS) |
| Cut A, Block 3: GSI | Done (CONUS, 8 variants; checked against the GSI Scout model) |
| Cut A clustering: A1, A2 and A3 (Blocks 1–3) | Done; A3 adds little to A2 |
| Cut B clustering of satellite curves | First runs done |
| Comparison with satellite curves and ground observations (NPN, live fuel moisture, iNaturalist) | Done; working regions chosen (A2, 13 regions nested in 7) |
| Phenology model tests by region | Done: GSI threshold tuning, curing forms, two curing targets, a soil-water bucket, a weather adjustment of the typical date; each scored against satellite dates and then checked against NPN grass sites |
| Curing and green-up rules | Final after the ground checks (October 13); packaged as typical-date maps and a yearly adjustment run (October 15) |
| NPN curing study (models fitted to ground dates) | Started October 15; first model comparison October 16 |

: Pipeline status {.striped}

**What we have found so far (October 2026).**

- **Regions:** climate regions (A2, 13 regions nested in 7) describe where herbaceous fuels
  share a seasonal timing better than location alone, and the satellite curves and ground
  observations agree on that.
- **Rules within regions:** every weather-driven rule we tried (the GSI with its thresholds
  tuned per region, a soil-water bucket, the typical date shifted by recent weather) could
  beat each place's typical date when scored against satellite dates. Checked against NPN
  grass sites, most did worse than the typical date. The exception: shifting the typical
  curing date by weather known two weeks ahead helps in the monsoon Southwest and,
  on few sites, the California annual grasslands.
- **What that means:** for now the typical date is the honest baseline for grass green-up
  and curing in most regions. A rule tuned to satellite dates needs a ground check before
  it is used, and the next round of curing rules should be fitted to ground observations
  directly. [Typical date plus a weather adjustment](#typical-date-plus-a-weather-adjustment)
  and the two sections after it have the details.
- **Fitted to the ground (first result, October 16):** models fitted to NPN grass dates
  directly, from one weather driver up to a random forest, also do no better than each
  grass's typical date. Much of the year-to-year scatter in single-plant dates is not
  shared between species at a site, which caps what any weather model can explain.
  [Fitting to the ground](#fitting-to-the-ground-the-npn-curing-study-first-result) has
  the details.

## Why regions?

The Growing Season Index (GSI; Jolly et al. 2005) in the National Fire Danger Rating
System turns daily minimum temperature, vapor pressure deficit and day length into an
index of plant activity, which is then mapped to live fuel moisture. The same
thresholds are applied everywhere, but herbaceous fuels in a desert grassland watered by
the summer monsoon, a shortgrass prairie, and a California annual grassland respond to
different cues on different calendars.

In discussions with fire managers and planners, the need that came up was **fuel
phenology regionalization**: a data-driven way to find regions with roughly common
green-up, maintenance and curing patterns, so that phenology models can be built and
tuned within each one. We start with **herbaceous fuels** and draw regions **wall to
wall across CONUS**. That way they can be tested anywhere, including in the East where
land-cover maps are challenging, and ground observations anywhere can be used. The
regions can later roll up to the two NFDRS live fuel classes.

## How the analysis is built

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 7
%%{init: {"themeVariables": {"fontSize": "17px"}}}%%
flowchart LR
  P["Daily PRISM 4 km<br/>ppt, tmin, tmax, vpdmax<br/>2001–2025"] --> B1["Block 1<br/>seasonal climate"]
  P --> B2["Block 2<br/>timing and variability"]
  P --> B3["Block 3<br/>GSI sub-indices"]
  B1 --> A["Cut A<br/>climate regions"]
  B2 --> A
  B3 --> A
  M["MODIS NDVI and NDII7<br/>Terra + Aqua, 1 km to 4 km"] --> C["Cut B<br/>seasonal-curve regions"]
  N["NLCD herbaceous cover"] -. "weights and mask" .-> A
  N -. "selects grass-dominated cells" .-> C
  A --> X{"Compare"}
  C --> X
  O["NPN and iNaturalist<br/>phenophase observations"] --> X
  X --> R["Fuel phenology regions<br/>for regional phenology models"]
```

Everything sits on the PRISM 4 km grid (about 480,000 land cells). Features are
computed **for each year and then summarized across years** (median and year-to-year
spread), never from an average-year climate: the GSI of an average year is not the
average GSI.

**From regions to rules.** Within the working regions, candidate rules for herbaceous
green-up and curing are tested in four steps; tabs 10 and 12–17 of [How the numbers
work](#how-the-numbers-work) show each score on toy data.

1. **Fit on half the years, score on the other half.** On 4,000 grass- and shrub-dominated
   cells with daily PRISM, every rule is fitted per region on odd years and scored on even
   years, then the reverse: mean absolute error in days against the satellite dates, each
   error capped at 90 days. Where a rule gives no date, the cell's typical date stands in.
2. **Compare with the typical date.** Each cell's median date over the fitting years is
   the bar every rule must clear.
3. **Check the satellite target against the ground.** Satellite dates are compared with NPN
   grass observations at the same cell and year: one row per site and year, dates on a
   circular year, more than 90 days apart counted as a season mismatch.
4. **Check each rule against the ground.** The rule is applied at the NPN sites' cells as
   fitted and compared with the ground dates in held-out years, after removing each site's
   average offset from the satellite: does the rule move each year toward the ground's
   early or late year?

### Data

| Data set | What it provides | Resolution and period |
|---|---|---|
| PRISM daily (Oregon State University) | Precipitation, min and max temperature, max vapor pressure deficit | 4 km, daily, 2001–2025 |
| MODIS MOD13A2 (Terra) and MYD13A2 (Aqua), Collection 6.1, via NASA AppEEARS | NDVI (greenness); NIR and MIR reflectance for NDII7 (canopy water and curing) | 1 km, 16-day composites, averaged to 4 km; 2001–2025 (Aqua from mid-2002) |
| Annual NLCD Collection 1 (USGS) | Grassland, shrub/scrub, pasture, crop shares per 4 km cell | 30 m land cover for 2001, 2012 and 2024 |
| USA-NPN and iNaturalist | Ground observations of phenophases (green-up, flowering, senescence) | Point observations, CONUS |

: Data sets {.striped}

## Study domain and herbaceous cover

Regions cover all CONUS land. Herbaceous cover from Annual NLCD is used to **describe and
weight** cells, not to define the domain. Two shares are kept: a *core* share
(grassland plus shrub/scrub) and an *open* share that adds pasture and hay, which is the
main herbaceous cover in the East. A **strict mask** (core share at least half of the land
and crops under a quarter) picks out the cells where a MODIS curve is mostly a
herbaceous signal. It is used to select Cut B curves and for sensitivity runs.

```{r fig-domain}
#| results: asis
show_fig("domain",
  "Herbaceous cover on the 4 km grid from Annual NLCD (mean of 2001, 2012 and 2024). The strict mask covers about a third of CONUS land, almost all of it in the West and Great Plains.",
  "Three maps of CONUS: core herbaceous share, open herbaceous share, and the strict herbaceous mask.")
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" collapse="true"}
## Why grassland and shrub are combined
In NLCD the split between grassland/herbaceous and shrub/scrub changes abruptly at
some state lines (for example Wyoming/Nebraska, Colorado/Kansas, New Mexico/Texas),
a mapping artifact rather than a real change in vegetation. The analysis therefore only
uses the combined share, never grassland alone.
:::

## Cut A: climate features

The climate features come in three blocks, which are added one at a time so we can see
what each contributes: **A1** = Block 1 + elevation and latitude, **A2** = A1 + Block 2,
**A3** = A2 + Block 3. Keeping the GSI-based features in their own block answers a
practical question: does the GSI formulation add information about where phenology
differs, or do its thresholds steer the regions?

### Block 1: seasonal climate (built)

The year runs from October through September (a *water year*) for temperature,
precipitation and aridity, because cool-season moisture comes before the green-up it
feeds. Freeze dates and growing degree days use the calendar year.

| Feature | Definition |
|---|---|
| Seasonal and annual temperature | Mean of daily (tmin + tmax)/2 for Oct–Dec, Jan–Mar, Apr–Jun, Jul–Sep and the water year; warmest-minus-coolest season range |
| Annual precipitation and seasonal shares | Water-year total and the fraction falling in each season (Jul–Sep isolates the monsoon; Apr–Jun the dry foresummer) |
| Aridity index | Precipitation / potential evapotranspiration (Hargreaves), for the water year and the warm season (Apr–Sep) |
| Freeze dates and freeze-free season | Last spring and first fall day with tmin ≤ 0 °C, and the days between them; ≤ −2.2 °C as a sensitivity check |
| Growing degree days | Base 5 °C (cool-season and general growth) and base 10 °C (warm-season grasses) |

: Block 1 features (21 per year) {.striped}

```{r fig-block1-medians}
#| results: asis
show_fig("block1_medians",
  "Six of the Block 1 features, as the median across years.",
  "Six maps of Block 1 climate features: mean annual temperature, annual precipitation, July to September share of precipitation, aridity index, freeze-free season length, and growing degree days above 10 C.")
```

How a feature varies **from year to year** matters as much as its typical value:
grasses in a place where summer rain is unreliable behave differently from grasses
where it always arrives. Block 1 keeps the spread (interquartile range, IQR) of every
feature alongside its median.

```{r fig-block1-iqr}
#| results: asis
show_fig("block1_iqr",
  "Year-to-year spread of three Block 1 features (interquartile range across years; precipitation as IQR relative to the median).",
  "Three maps of year-to-year variability: annual precipitation, July to September share of precipitation, and freeze-free season length.")
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Reading the preliminary maps
- Medians and spreads are across water years 2002–2025.
- Where no freeze occurs, the freeze-free season is set to the full year. Along the
  California coast, south Texas and Florida, years with and without a freeze mix, which
  shows up as a large year-to-year spread in freeze-free season length.
- The aridity index is very skewed (most of the West is well below 1), so it is
  log-transformed before clustering (as are annual precipitation and warm-season aridity).
:::

### Block 2: timing and variability (built)

Herbaceous phenology responds to the **timing and reliability** of moisture and warmth,
not just the averages. Block 2 is computed per year from daily PRISM and summarized as the
median, the year-to-year spread, and coefficients of variation.

| Feature | Definition |
|---|---|
| Warm-season rain onset | First wet day from May 1 that starts a 10-day total of at least 20 mm, with no dry spell of 20 days or more in the following 30 days; no onset by September 30 is recorded as "no onset" (and the share of years with an onset is kept) |
| Rain pulses | Days with at least 5 mm in the warm (Apr–Sep) and cool (Oct–Mar) seasons; 2.5 and 10 mm as sensitivity checks |
| Dry spells | Longest warm-season run of days under 1 mm, and the number of warm-season dry spells of 20 days or more |
| False starts | Growing degree days (base 5 °C) accumulated before the last spring hard freeze (≤ −2.2 °C) |
| Limiting factor | Share of the water year's days that are cold-limited (daily mean temperature under 5 °C) or, on the other days, moisture-limited (precipitation over the past 30 days under half of potential evapotranspiration over the same days) |
| Year-to-year variability | Coefficient of variation of annual and warm-season precipitation; standard deviation of Apr–Jun temperature |

: Block 2 features {.striped}

### Block 3: the Growing Season Index (built)

The daily GSI is computed for every year and grid cell from PRISM, with the same model code
as the project's GSI Scout tool. It serves two purposes: features for the A3 regions (when
the season starts, peaks and ends; which factor limits it), and the model whose regional
tuning the regions are meant for.

| Choice | Variants |
|---|---|
| Parameter sets | **National literature defaults** (NFDRS 2016: VPD 900–4,100 Pa, daylength 10–11 h, 21-day smoothing, green-up at 0.5) and **FEMS operational values** (VPD 1,956–3,882 Pa, daylength 11–12 h, 28-day smoothing, green-up at 0.3); minimum temperature −2 to 5 °C in both |
| Moisture | None, a 28-day precipitation sum (0–10 mm literature, 10–20 mm FEMS), or the Keetch–Byram Drought Index (limiting from 200, fully at 600) |
| Sensitivity | Without the VPD ramp (PRISM VPD is its least reliable variable) |

: GSI variants {.striped}

PRISM has no soil moisture, so the soil-moisture option of GSI Scout is not used here.

**A3 regions.** A3 adds the GSI as a third block of equal weight to A2's climate
and timing features. It is clustered with the FEMS operational settings and the 28-day
precipitation ramp (the GSI as run today), and repeated without the VPD ramp and with the
KBDI ramp. Four GSI feature groups share the block equally:

- timing: green-up, peak and curing dates;
- year-to-year spread of green-up and curing;
- activity: mean GSI, days in the green phase, number of green-up pulses;
- the share of the year limited by each factor.

If A3 explains the satellite curves and ground dates better than A2, the GSI is adding
something the climate features miss. If not, its thresholds may be steering the regions.

**What A3 shows (October 10).** The GSI features neither add to nor steer the regions much:

- A3 and A2 draw largely the same regions (adjusted Rand index 0.71–0.80 at 7, 10 and 13
  regions).
- On the timing of the satellite curves in herbaceous cells they are tied (A3 51, 54, 57 %
  at 7, 10, 13 regions; A2 49, 53, 55 %). On the curves as observed, A3 is lower at 13
  regions (42 against 50 %).
- Against the ground observations, every A3-minus-A2 range spans zero except a small gain
  for the woody live fuel moisture peak at 7 regions. Year-to-year synchrony is the same.
- A3 is less stable than A2 (0.74 against 0.83 at 7 regions). Dropping the VPD ramp or
  using KBDI changes little.

The GSI is built from the same temperature, daylength and precipitation the climate blocks
already describe, so it mostly repeats them. A2 stays the working set of regions.

## Cut B: satellite seasonal curves

Cut B uses MODIS 16-day composites from both Terra and Aqua at 1 km, averaged to the
4 km grid using only good-quality pixels. The count of valid pixels and the share
flagged as snow are kept for every composite. Two indices describe the season:

- **NDVI** for greenness;
- **NDII7** = (NIR − MIR) / (NIR + MIR) for canopy water content. It drops as grasses
  cure, often separating from NDVI when plants are still green but drying.

```{r fig-cutb-curves}
#| results: asis
show_fig("cutb_curves",
  "16-day NDVI and NDII7 at sample grassland locations, Terra and Aqua.",
  "Time series of NDVI and NDII7 at sample grassland locations, with Terra and Aqua shown as separate lines.")
```

```{r fig-cutb-peak}
#| results: asis
show_fig("cutb_peak",
  "Size of the NDVI seasonal cycle and when it peaks, from one year of Terra composites. Cells with an amplitude under 0.1 have no clear green season.",
  "Two maps: NDVI seasonal amplitude, and the timing of peak NDVI in three seasons.")
```

For each year the two sensors are merged (Terra reads slightly higher than Aqua in
NDII7, so the median difference per cell is split between them), composites with too few
good pixels or too much snow are dropped, and a weighted smoother that follows the upper
envelope of the data (clouds and snow pull values down) gives a curve every 8 days from
October of the previous year through March of the next. From those curves come green-up,
peak, end of season and curing dates, amplitudes, and the median curve across years that
the clustering uses. Cut B is run two ways: on the curves as they are (**level + shape**:
how green and when) and on curves rescaled by their own amplitude (**timing only**).

## First regions and how well they work

Both cuts were clustered with k-means for 4 to 20 regions (Cut A up to 30). Within a block,
features are grouped (for Block 1: temperature, moisture amount, seasonality) and each
group gets equal weight, so the eight temperature features don't outvote the rest. Seven
regions is where the A2 climate regions are most stable under resampling; around 13 the
climate regions begin to split the tallgrass prairie from the northern Midwest and the
California annual grasslands from the Mojave. The comparisons below led to the working
regions chosen on October 9: **A2 at 13 regions, nested into A2 at 7** (see
[What the candidate regions look like](#what-the-candidate-regions-look-like)).

```{r fig-regions}
#| results: asis
show_fig("regions",
  "First climate (top) and satellite-curve (bottom) regions. Region colours are matched to the first map where regions overlap, so the same colour across maps means mostly the same area. Climate regions are smooth by construction; satellite regions follow land cover and are patchier.",
  "Six maps of CONUS regions: climate A1 with 10 regions, climate A2 with 7 and 13 regions, satellite-curve regions with 7 and 13 regions, and timing-only satellite regions with 13 regions.")
```

### Do climate regions explain the satellite curves?

For each set of regions, the share of the variation in the median satellite curves
(NDVI and NDII7) that lies *between* regions rather than within them. This is scored twice:
on the curves as observed, where how green a place gets dominates, and on the curves
scaled by their own seasonal amplitude, which leaves only **timing** (when green-up, peak
and curing happen), the part that matters most for regional phenology models. The satellite
regions are fitted to these curves, so they show roughly how much any set of that size
can explain. The *location only* baseline divides the map into compact blobs with no
climate information: a useful set of regions has to beat it.

```{r fig-eval-curves}
#| results: asis
show_fig("eval_curves",
  "Share of the satellite-curve variance explained by each set of regions, by number of regions: curves as observed (top) and timing only (bottom). Dashed vertical lines mark 7, 10 and 13 regions.",
  "Four line charts of variance explained versus number of regions, for all cells and for the strict herbaceous mask, one line per set of regions.")
```

### Do the regions separate observed phenology on the ground?

Ground observations come from three sources: USA-NPN observations of grasses (percent
green canopy, giving green-up, curing and cured dates) and other plants (leaf onset and
end), the Globe-LFMC live fuel moisture database (date of the seasonal peak and of the
50 % decline), and iNaturalist flowering records. Each site (one plant type at one place)
is reduced to its median date across years. The score is the adjusted R-squared of those
dates on region: how much of the spread in dates is between regions, with a penalty for
using more regions.

```{r fig-eval-obs}
#| results: asis
show_fig("eval_obs",
  "How well each set of regions separates observed dates (adjusted R-squared of site median dates on region), by number of regions. Bars at 7, 10 and 13 regions show the range over 90 % of block resamples of the sites.",
  "Six line charts of adjusted R-squared versus number of regions for NPN grass green-up, curing and cured dates, live fuel moisture peaks for herbaceous and woody fuels, and iNaturalist flowering onset.")
```

```{r tbl-eval}
#| results: asis
es <- NULL
for (pr in c("full", "dev")) {
  f <- sprintf("figs/eval_summary_%s.csv", pr)
  if (file.exists(f)) { es <- utils::read.csv(f, stringsAsFactors = FALSE); break }
}
if (!is.null(es)) {
  plab <- c(A1_groups = "Climate A1", A2_groups = "Climate A2", A2_herbw = "Climate A2, herb-weighted",
            A3_groups = "Climate A3 (+ GSI)", B_raw = "Satellite (level + shape)",
            B_shape = "Satellite (timing only)", geo = "Location only")
  clab <- c(curves_all = "Curves, all cells", curves_herb = "Curves, herb mask",
            timing_all = "Timing, all cells", timing_herb = "Timing, herb mask",
            grass_greenup = "Grass green-up", grass_curing = "Grass curing", grass_cured = "Grass cured",
            lfmc_herb_peak = "LFMC herb peak", lfmc_woody_peak = "LFMC woody peak",
            inat_flower = "iNat flowering")
  es$partition <- ifelse(es$partition %in% names(plab), plab[es$partition], es$partition)
  num <- setdiff(names(es), c("partition", "k"))
  es[num] <- lapply(es[num], function(v) sprintf("%.2f", v))
  names(es) <- c("Regions", "k", ifelse(num %in% names(clab), clab[num], num))
  cat(knitr::kable(es, align = c("l", "r", rep("r", length(num))),
                   caption = "Scores at 7, 10 and 13 regions: share of satellite-curve variance explained, and adjusted R-squared of observed dates on region"),
      sep = "\n")
} else {
  cat('\n::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}\n## Table pending\nScores at 7, 10 and 13 regions.\n:::\n\n')
}
```

```{r tbl-eval-diff}
#| results: asis
ed <- NULL
for (pr in c("full", "dev")) {
  f <- sprintf("figs/eval_diff_%s.csv", pr)
  if (file.exists(f)) { ed <- utils::read.csv(f, stringsAsFactors = FALSE); break }
}
if (!is.null(ed)) {
  ed$cell <- sprintf("%+.2f (%+.2f to %+.2f)", ed$diff, ed$lo, ed$hi)
  w <- stats::reshape(ed[, c("set", "comparison", "k", "cell")], idvar = c("set", "comparison"),
                      timevar = "k", direction = "wide")
  names(w) <- sub("^cell\\.", "", names(w))
  names(w)[1:2] <- c("Observations", "Comparison")
  names(w)[-(1:2)] <- paste(names(w)[-(1:2)], "regions")
  cat('\n::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" collapse="true"}\n## How sure are these differences?\n',
      'Differences in adjusted R-squared between two sets of regions, scored on the same resampled sites. ',
      'Sites are resampled in 2-degree blocks, because nearby sites are not independent; the range covers ',
      '90 % of 500 resamples. A range that spans zero means the observations cannot tell the two apart.\n\n', sep = "")
  cat(knitr::kable(w, row.names = FALSE, align = c("l", "l", rep("r", ncol(w) - 2))), sep = "\n")
  cat("\n:::\n\n")
}
```

### Do cells in a region move together from year to year?

A region is a good domain for a phenology model when its cells green up and cure early or
late in the same years, not only when their average seasons match. For each cell and year,
the satellite green-up, peak, end-of-season and curing dates are expressed as departures
from that cell's own typical date, and the score is the share of those departures that the
region's average departure in the same year accounts for. One CONUS-wide region is the
baseline.

```{r fig-eval-sync}
#| results: asis
show_fig("eval_sync",
  "Share of year-to-year departures in satellite season dates that cells share with their region, by number of regions (herbaceous cells). The dotted line is one region for all of CONUS.",
  "Four line charts of year-to-year synchrony versus number of regions, for green-up, peak, end of season and curing.")
```

**Reading the synchrony scores.**

- **Most year-to-year variation is local.** Even at 20 regions, a region's average departure
  accounts for only about a quarter of the cells' year-to-year departures in green-up and
  peak, and about a sixth for curing. One CONUS-wide region accounts for 3–11 %. A
  phenology model that only knows a region's typical season will miss most of a given
  year; it needs that year's local weather, which is what the GSI supplies.
- **Climate regions capture more of it than location alone,** most clearly for the NDVI
  peak and curing (at 13 regions: 0.20–0.22 against 0.16 for the peak, 0.14–0.16 against
  0.12 for curing). The level + shape satellite regions do worst: grouping cells by how
  green they get says little about whether they vary together.
- **The gains continue past 13 regions** without levelling off, slowly. Herbaceous-weighted
  A2 is slightly ahead at 13 regions for green-up (0.27 against 0.24–0.26 for A1 and A2).
- **Synchrony differs a lot between regions.** In A2 at 13 regions, cells move together
  in the Southeast (1), the mid-South (5), the upper Midwest (13) and the low deserts' peak
  (4) (shared share 0.35–0.65), but hardly at all in the interior West (6, 12) and the
  monsoon Southwest's curing (3) (about 0.1). Those are regions where the season follows
  scattered storms, so neighboring cells can have quite different years.

### Does tuning the GSI by region predict green-up and curing better?

This is the test the regions are for. On a sample of 4,000 grass- and shrub-dominated cells,
the GSI's thresholds (minimum temperature, VPD, the start of the daylength ramp and a
moisture ramp) are fitted to the satellite green-up and curing dates: once for all of
CONUS, and separately for each region (the first run at 7, 10 and 13 regions, the second at
7 and 13). The fits use half of the years and are scored on the other half, against the
national default settings and against simply predicting each cell's typical date. Tab 10
of [How the numbers work](#how-the-numbers-work) shows the scores on a small example.

```{r fig-gsi-model}
#| results: asis
show_fig("gsi_model",
  "Error in predicted green-up and curing dates on held-out years (top) and how well each model tracks early and late years (bottom), for GSI thresholds fitted per region, fitted once for CONUS, the national default settings, and each cell's typical date.",
  "Four charts comparing GSI model versions by number of regions: green-up and curing date error, and correlation of yearly departures.")
```

**Reading the model test.** The test was run twice: first with the 28-day precipitation
ramp only, then with a longer threshold search and three moisture options (28-day
precipitation, the Keetch-Byram Drought Index, none), keeping for each region the option
that fit its fitting years best. The second run confirms the first.

- **Tuning by region pays off against the national defaults.** For green-up, thresholds
  fitted per region miss by 28–29 days on average (median about 14), against 32 days for
  one CONUS-wide fit and 37–41 days for the FEMS and NFDRS defaults (median 23–29). For
  curing the gain is smaller: 52–55 days against 59–62.
- **The number of regions makes almost no difference.** Errors at 7 and 13 regions are
  within about a day of each other for every set of regions.
- **Moisture matters, and KBDI fits most regions best.** Without a moisture ramp the
  fitted GSI is consistently worse. KBDI was the best option in about two thirds of the
  regions, and it roughly doubles the (still small) skill for curing.
- **The GSI now matches, but does not beat, a cell's typical date.** Predicting each cell's
  usual green-up misses by 27 days; the best regional fits miss by 27–29. For curing the
  typical date is still better (48 days against 52–55). How well the models track early
  and late years improved with KBDI (correlations of about 0.35–0.48 for green-up,
  0.11–0.14 for curing), but remains modest.
- **What that means.** Tuning thresholds by region moves the GSI's average timing onto the
  observed season, and a drought-based moisture ramp adds some year-to-year skill, but the
  index's form limits how well it follows curing. A longer search did not change that, so
  it is not a fitting artifact. Part of the remaining gap is noise in the satellite dates
  themselves and the local nature of yearly variation (see the synchrony results above).

```{r tbl-gsi-moist}
#| results: asis
gmf <- NULL
for (pr in c("full", "dev")) {
  f <- sprintf("figs/gsi_model_moist_%s.csv", pr)
  if (file.exists(f)) { gmf <- utils::read.csv(f, check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE); break }
}
if (!is.null(gmf)) {
  cat(knitr::kable(gmf, align = c("l", rep("r", ncol(gmf) - 1)),
                   caption = "Mean absolute error on held-out years, green-up / curing (days), by moisture option"), sep = "\n")
  cat("\n\n")
}
```

### Does changing the GSI's form help with curing?

The model test showed that curing is limited by the GSI's form, not by the regions or the
fitting. The next test keeps the same sample, years and scoring, uses the working regions
(A2 at 7 and 13 regions plus one CONUS-wide fit), and changes the model in two ways, every
combination fitted:

- **Moisture memory:** the KBDI ramp (best in the first test), a 30-day mean of KBDI, and
  60- and 90-day precipitation sums. A longer memory lets a dry spell build up before the
  index drops.
- **How green-up and curing dates are read from the index:**
  - *Share of the season:* green-up at 20 % and curing at 50 % of the season's range, as
    for the satellite curves (the first test).
  - *Share of the season, fitted:* the same, with the two shares fitted separately.
  - *NFDRS4 levels:* fixed GSI levels as in the NFDRS4 code. Herbs green up when the GSI
    passes the green-up threshold, and are half cured when it falls to halfway between
    that threshold and 1 (NFDRS4's cured share is (1 − GSI) / (1 − threshold)).
  - *GSI levels, fitted:* separate green-up and curing levels fitted.

The bar to clear is the cell's typical curing date (48 days), and a real gain in tracking
early and late years.

```{r fig-gsi-curing}
#| results: asis
if (file.exists("figs/gsi_curing_full.png")) {
  show_fig("gsi_curing",
    "Error in predicted green-up and curing dates on held-out years and how well curing tracks early and late years, for each GSI form fitted once for CONUS and per working region. Dashed line: each cell's typical date.",
    "Dot charts comparing GSI forms: green-up error, curing error and correlation of yearly curing departures.")
  for (f in c("gsi_curing_full.csv", "gsi_curing_best_full.csv")) if (file.exists(file.path("figs", f))) {
    tb <- utils::read.csv(file.path("figs", f), check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
    cat(knitr::kable(tb, align = c("l", rep("r", ncol(tb) - 1)),
                     caption = if (grepl("best", f)) "Which form fits each region best (fitting years)" else
                       "Green-up / curing error (days), curing correlation and share of curing dates produced, by form"), sep = "\n")
    cat("\n\n")
  }
} else cat("*Results to come.*\n\n")
```

**Reading the curing test.** The test was run twice. The first run counted a missing GSI
date as a fixed 60-day miss, and fits in hard regions learned to give no curing date
(the scoring flaw is explained in tab 10 of [How the numbers work](#how-the-numbers-work)).
The rerun, shown here, uses the cell's typical date wherever the GSI gives none, so skipping
can never beat the baseline. It also searches longer (no fit ran out of search) and drops
the two moisture terms that never won the first time (30-day mean KBDI, 60-day
precipitation). The two runs agree on where the GSI works.

- **Nationally, curing does not beat the typical date.** With the best form per region at
  13 regions the error is 47.8 days against 48.3. Much of that is fallback: the best forms
  date curing themselves in only about 38 % of cell-years. On the years they do date, the
  GSI and the typical date are tied (40 against 41 days). Forms that always give a curing
  date (share of the season) miss by 51–53 days, 5–7 days more than the typical date on the
  same years.
- **The fits switch the GSI's curing date off where it cannot help.** A fit that gives no
  date scores exactly like the typical date, so in five regions the best fits produce
  curing dates in under 1 % of cell-years. That is itself a map of where the GSI's curing
  logic fails.
- **Green-up does slightly better than the typical date** with a 90-day precipitation
  memory: 25 days against 27 overall, 23 against 25 on the years the GSI dates, and a
  correlation of about 0.4 with early and late years.

| Region (13 regions) | Curing: GSI vs typical date (days) | Curing dated by GSI | Curing correlation | Green-up: GSI vs typical date (days) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2, southern Plains | **39 vs 45** | 97 % | 0.33 | **25 vs 32** |
| 5, mid-South (with the tallgrass prairie) | **16 vs 20** | all years | 0.71 | 9 vs 7 |
| 13, upper Midwest | **20 vs 23** | all years | 0.34 | **8 vs 9** |
| 4, low deserts | 42 vs 44 | 90 % | 0.23 | **40 vs 62** |
| 10, northern and central Great Plains | 44 vs 42 | 80 % | 0.14 | 12 vs 10 |
| 3, monsoon Southwest | switched off (58 vs 49) | 0 % | | 38 vs 6 |
| 12, southern Great Basin and Colorado Plateau | switched off (72 vs 61) | 0 % | | 56 vs 36 |
| 11, California annual grasslands | switched off (36 vs 24) | 0 % | | **33 vs 40** |
| 6, Snake River Plain and northern Great Basin | switched off (78 vs 63) | 0 % | | 33 vs 30 |
| 7, Rockies | switched off (59 vs 38) | 0 % | | 14 vs 13 |

: GSI vs each cell's typical date by region, on the years the GSI gives a date (rerun). Where the best fit gives no curing dates, the numbers in brackets are for the KBDI form that always gives one. Regions 1, 8 and 9 have too few sampled cells for their own fit. Corrected October 12: this table first showed the clustering's internal region numbers under the map's region names. {.striped}

- **What that means.** With tuned thresholds the GSI beats the typical NDII7 curing date and
  follows early and late years in the southern Plains, the mid-South and the upper Midwest:
  warm-season grasslands whose curing comes with late-summer drought or fall cold. It ties
  in the low deserts and does worse in the Great Plains. Elsewhere the fits switch it off:
  - in the monsoon Southwest grasses can green up twice a year, so the satellite curing
    date itself jumps between spring and late summer;
  - in the California annual grasslands growth comes in the cool season, which the
    temperature and daylength ramps hold back;
  - in the interior West (Snake River Plain, southern Great Basin and Colorado Plateau) and
    the Rockies the season is short, and the target check below found that the NDII7 curing
    date there often picks a different season from the ground (61–96 % of site-years at the
    few grass sites).

  For green-up the GSI helps most in the low deserts, the California grasslands and the
  southern Plains, and fails in the monsoon Southwest and the southern Great Basin.
- **Which forms win.** For curing, KBDI wins most regions (25 of 34 region-folds at 7 and 13
  regions), most often read at NFDRS4's fixed levels or with fitted shares of the season. For
  green-up, the 90-day precipitation sum is best.

### Does a different curing target change the picture?

The target check below found that NDVI end of season (the date greenness falls back below
half its seasonal range) matches the timing of ground curing at least as well as NDII7 curing, and picks
the wrong season less often. So the curing test was run once more, scoring the GSI against
NDVI end of season instead, with the four forms that won most often against NDII7.

```{r fig-gsi-curing-eos50}
#| results: asis
if (file.exists("figs/gsi_curing_eos50_full.png")) {
  show_fig("gsi_curing_eos50",
    "As the figure above, with NDVI end of season as the curing target. Dashed line: each cell's typical date.",
    "Dot charts comparing GSI forms against NDVI end of season: green-up error, curing error and correlation of yearly departures.")
} else cat("*Results to come.*\n\n")
```

- **The target is steadier, but the GSI still only ties the typical date.** Each cell's
  typical end-of-season date misses by 29 days (against 48 for NDII7 curing), so this target
  varies less from year to year. The best regional fits also miss by 29 days, and on the
  years they date themselves the GSI and the typical date are tied (30 against 30 days at 13
  regions).
- **The GSI tracks early and late years better against this target**: correlations of about
  0.36–0.37 at 7 and 13 regions, against 0.15–0.21 for NDII7 curing. The GSI follows the
  decline in greenness more closely than the decline in canopy water.
- **The regional pattern holds.** Against NDVI end of season the GSI beats the typical date in
  the mid-South (15 against 17 days, correlation 0.72) and the southern Plains (33 against
  44), ties in the upper Midwest and the low deserts, does worse in the Great Plains (30
  against 27) and the Rockies (37 against 24), and the fits switch it off in the monsoon
  Southwest, the California annual grasslands, the Snake River Plain and the southern Great
  Basin.
- **What that means.** The failures are not an artifact of the satellite target: with either
  target, the GSI's form does not fit the seasons of the monsoon Southwest, the California
  grasslands and the interior West. Those regions need a different model form.

### A different model form: a soil-water bucket

Where the GSI fails, its form may not fit the season: its temperature and daylength ramps
hold back cool-season growth, and its 28–90-day moisture terms forget a wet winter. Two
alternatives were fitted and scored exactly as above, against both curing targets:

- **A daily soil-water bucket.** Rain fills it, and evapotranspiration (Hargreaves, from
  daily minimum and maximum temperature) drains it in proportion to how full it is. The
  index is a ramp on how full the bucket is, times a minimum-temperature ramp for cold
  places; there is no VPD or daylength term. The bucket size is fitted (10–400 mm; the fits
  settle around 180–200 mm).
- **Season-aware reading of dates**, for two-season climates: the season's peak is looked
  for within 75 days of the cell's usual mid-season (learned from the fitting years only),
  instead of taking the year's highest point. Tried with the bucket and with the GSI's best
  moisture terms.

```{r fig-gsi-curing-newforms}
#| results: asis
for (nm in c("gsi_curing_eos50_newforms", "gsi_curing_newforms")) if (file.exists(sprintf("figs/%s_full.png", nm))) {
  show_fig(nm, if (grepl("eos50", nm))
      "Soil-water bucket and season-aware forms, scored against NDVI end of season. Dashed line: each cell's typical date." else
      "The same, scored against NDII7 curing.",
    "Dot charts comparing the soil-water bucket and season-aware forms: green-up error, curing error and correlation of yearly departures.")
}
```

- **The bucket is the first form to beat the typical date nationally**, though narrowly.
  Against NDVI end of season, the best form per region misses by 28 days at 13 regions
  (27.7 at 7) against 29 for the typical date and 29 for the GSI. On the years it dates
  itself, 27.5 against 29.0 days, and it tracks early and late years about as well as the
  GSI (correlation 0.36–0.44). Against NDII7 curing the gain is about one day (47.5 against
  48.3). The bucket wins about three of every four region-folds.
- **It helps green-up most**: 25 days against 27 for the typical date and 26 for the GSI,
  with a correlation of about 0.5 with early and late years. The gains are largest where
  green-up follows rain rather than spring warmth: the California annual grasslands (30
  against 40 days), the monsoon Southwest (27 against 35) and the southern Plains (24
  against 33).
- **For curing it helps where the GSI already did, and in the monsoon Southwest a little.**
  Against NDVI end of season:

| Region (13 regions) | Curing: typical / GSI / bucket (days) | Bucket dates curing | Green-up: typical / GSI / bucket (days) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2, southern Plains | 44 / **33** / **33** | 98 % | 33 / 26 / **24** |
| 3, monsoon Southwest | 29 / off / **28** | all years | 35 / 35 / **27** |
| 4, low deserts | 29 / 30 / 29 | 94 % | 62 / 39 / **38** |
| 5, mid-South (with the tallgrass prairie) | 17 / 15 / **14** | all years | **7** / 8 / 9 |
| 6, Snake River Plain and northern Great Basin | 26 / off / off | 0 % | **30** / 32 / 34 |
| 7, Rockies | 24 / 37 / 31 | 50 % | **13** / 14 / 18 |
| 10, northern and central Great Plains | 27 / 30 / 27 | all years | **10** / 11 / 13 |
| 11, California annual grasslands | 17 / off / 21 | 93 % | 40 / 40 / **30** |
| 12, southern Great Basin and Colorado Plateau | 38 / off / off | 0 % | 44 / 44 / 44 |
| 13, upper Midwest | 19 / 19 / 19 | all years | 9 / 8 / 8 |

: Each cell's typical date, the best GSI form and the best new form, by region (error in days on held-out years, NDVI end of season as the curing target). "off" means the fits gave no dates and fell back to the typical date. Regions 1, 8 and 9 have too few sampled cells. Corrected October 12 (map region numbers; see the note under the first curing table). {.striped}

- **What that means.** With weather in these simple forms, curing is predicted better than
  by each place's typical date only in the southern Plains and the mid-South (and barely in
  the monsoon Southwest). In the California annual grasslands, the interior West, the
  Rockies, the Great Plains, the upper Midwest and the low deserts the typical date is as
  good or better. California annual grasses senesce after setting seed, which the GSI's
  ramps do not represent; in the interior West the satellite target itself is often in a
  different season from the ground.

  For green-up, the bucket adds skill in the California grasslands, the monsoon Southwest,
  the low deserts and the southern Plains; elsewhere the typical date is as good.

### Which weather cues go with early and late curing?

**Decision (October 11), under revision.** The decision set each place's **typical curing
date** as the baseline in the regions where no model beat it, and the GSI or bucket where
they did. It named the regions from the model tables above before they were corrected
(October 12): those tables had shown the clustering's internal region numbers under the
map's names. With the map numbers, the GSI or bucket beats the typical date in the southern
Plains and the mid-South (and barely in the monsoon Southwest); nothing beats it in the
California annual grasslands, the interior West, the Rockies, the Great Plains, the upper
Midwest or the low deserts. The cue screening and rule test below use the map numbers
throughout. A revised decision is proposed under [Typical date plus a weather
adjustment](#typical-date-plus-a-weather-adjustment).

Region-specific curing rules might still beat the typical date, but only if some weather cue
explains early and late curing years. Before building such rules, the
yearly departures of the satellite curing date from each cell's own mean are compared with
the yearly departures of candidate cues, region by region:

- the green-up date: does curing follow a fixed lag after green-up, as seed set in annual
  grasses would?
- summer rain onset and end;
- the last soaking spring rain;
- the first fall frost and hard freeze;
- spring and summer heat;
- rain by season;
- the longest summer dry spell.

Daylength cannot be a cue, because it is the same every year. For each region the screening
reports each cue's correlation, and the share of curing departures a small model of up to
three cues predicts in held-out years. Tab 15 of [How the numbers work](#how-the-numbers-work)
shows the calculation.

```{r fig-curing-cues}
#| results: asis
if (file.exists("figs/curing_cues_full.png")) {
  show_fig("curing_cues",
    "Correlation of yearly curing departures (NDVI end of season) with each cue's departures, by working region, and the share of the departures a small cue model predicts in held-out years (top row).",
    "Grid of correlations between curing departures and weather cues, one column per region, with a top row of predicted shares.")
  f <- "figs/curing_cues_full.csv"
  if (file.exists(f)) {
    tb <- utils::read.csv(f, check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
    cat(knitr::kable(tb, align = c("l", "r", "r", "l"), caption = "Curing cue screening by region (NDVI end of season)"), sep = "\n")
    cat("\n\n")
  }
} else cat("*Results to come.*\n\n")
```

**Reading the cue screening (October 12).** The screening used the 4,000 sample cells and all
their years; regions 1, 8 and 9 have too few herbaceous sample cells to screen. A
share of 0.33 means a cue model removes a third of the variance of the yearly departures, so
their typical size falls by about a fifth (the square root of 0.67 is 0.82).

- **Weather cues explain little of the early and late curing years.** Across CONUS a
  three-cue model predicts 10 % of the departures in held-out years; within regions, 8–33 %.
  For comparison, where the bucket works best it does better: in the mid-South (5) its curing
  dates correlate 0.76 with the satellite's departures (more than half the variance), against
  25 % for the best cues.
- **The California annual grasslands (11) are the one clear case.** Cue models predict a
  third of the departures. A warm spring brings curing earlier (correlation −0.53); a wet
  cool season and late spring rain push it later (0.37 and 0.35). That is the expected story
  for annual grasses: they set seed and die as the soil dries, and spring heat and late rain
  shift when that happens. Here the satellite target is good too (89 % of site-years within
  30 days of the ground). A simple rule (the typical date shifted by spring temperature and
  cool-season and spring rain) could beat the typical date.
- **The mid-South (5) and the southern Plains (2) are marginal.** In the mid-South a hot
  summer brings curing earlier and summer rain delays it (25 % predicted), but only 63 sample
  cells are in the region, and the target check found that the satellite does not follow the
  ground's early and late years well there. In the southern Plains most of what is predicted (20 %)
  comes from the green-up date: a late spring means a late end of season. A rule there would
  add little beyond following green-up.
- **The monsoon Southwest (3) has no usable cue** (13 %; fall rain and the end of the summer
  rains delay curing a little). Its curing year to year is not explained by these cues, and a
  third of its satellite dates pick a different season from the ground. The typical date stays.
- **The low deserts (4) score fairly high (29 %)**, mostly from the green-up date and spring
  heat, but they have almost no ground sites to check the target against.
- **Elsewhere the pattern is consistent**: summer rain delays curing and summer heat
  advances it (the Great Plains, the mid-South, region 13), spring heat advances it in the
  West, and a late green-up means a late curing almost everywhere. These are the same signals
  the GSI and the bucket already use, which is why they work where they work.
- **With the NDII7 curing date as the target** the shares are lower nearly everywhere (CONUS
  6 %; monsoon Southwest 5 %), except the mid-South (37 %, with the same caveat).
- **Green-up** is predicted even less well by these cues (CONUS 5 %; at most 21 %, in the
  monsoon Southwest, from cool-season and spring rain).

So a region-specific curing rule looks worth trying only in the California annual
grasslands, and the screening flatters the cues: its seasonal windows include weather that
comes after curing (spring rain through June, for a mid-May curing date).

### Typical date plus a weather adjustment

**Decision (October 12).** One general rule is tested in every region, and kept only where it
beats the typical date: **each cell's typical curing date, shifted by a small weather
adjustment that uses only weather known before the date is needed.** This is the last curing
experiment; whatever it shows, the next step is writing up the operational recommendation
per region.

How it works:

- **Cutoff.** For each cell, the cues stop at its typical curing date minus a lead time: 14
  days is the operational case, and 0 and 30 days show how fast the signal fades.
- **Cues** (all ending at the cutoff): rain in the last 30, 90 and 180 days; mean daily
  maximum temperature in the last 30 and 60 days; dry days in the last 60; days since the last
  rain of 10 mm or more; and this year's satellite green-up date, if it came before the cutoff
  (otherwise it counts as typical).
- **Adjustment.** Each cue becomes a departure from the cell's own average; the adjustment is
  a linear model of up to three cue departures, picked on the fitting years and pooled over the
  region's cells, with no constant (no cue means no change). Adjustments are limited to ±60
  days.
- **Scoring.** Exactly as in the GSI tests: typical date = the cell's median over the fitting
  years (odd or even years); both the typical date and the adjusted date are scored on the
  other years by mean absolute error, each error capped at 90 days. Season jumps are left out
  of fitting but still scored.

Tab 16 of [How the numbers work](#how-the-numbers-work) shows the calculation on toy data.

```{r tab-curing-adjust}
#| results: asis
f <- "figs/curing_adjust_full.csv"
if (file.exists(f)) {
  tb <- utils::read.csv(f, check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  cat(knitr::kable(tb, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "l"),
                   caption = "Typical curing date against typical date plus weather adjustment (NDVI end of season), held-out years. Gain = typical-date error minus adjusted error (positive = the adjustment helps)."), sep = "\n")
  cat("\n\n")
} else cat("*Results to come.*\n\n")
```

**Reading the rule test (October 12).**

- **The adjustment beats the typical date in every region**, with weather that ends two
  weeks before the date. Across CONUS the error falls from 29.3 to 27.2 days; the gain is
  2.3 days with no lead and still 1.8 days with a 30-day lead, so most of the signal is in
  weather well before curing. Nationally that is better than the best GSI or bucket form per
  region (28 days). It does better than the cue screening suggested because its windows end
  at each cell's own typical date instead of fixed calendar seasons.
- **The gains are a few days**: largest in the southern Plains (4.6), the Great Plains (4.5),
  the low deserts (3.1), the upper Midwest (2.8) and the California annual grasslands (2.7,
  from 17 to 14 days); about a day in the monsoon Southwest, the southern Great Basin and the
  Rockies; and 0.3 days in the mid-South. About half of the held-out cell-years get closer
  and a third get further away; the adjusted dates follow early and late years with
  correlations of about 0.5 where the gains are largest.
- **The cues it picks make physical sense.** Warm weather in the last two months brings
  curing earlier (about 5–6 days per degree in the Great Plains, 2–3 in the California
  grasslands, 3–6 in the southern Plains); rain in the last one to three months delays it
  (about 0.1–0.3 days per mm); a long dry spell or a long time since the last soaking rain
  brings it earlier; and a late green-up means a late curing.
- **Against the model forms** (curing error in days, NDVI end of season):

| Region (13 regions) | Typical date | Best GSI | Best bucket | Typical date + adjustment (14-day lead) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2, southern Plains | 44 | **33** | **33** | 39 |
| 3, monsoon Southwest | 29 | off | **28** | **28** |
| 4, low deserts | 29 | 30 | 29 | **26** |
| 5, mid-South (with the tallgrass prairie) | 17 | 15 | **14** | 17 |
| 6, Snake River Plain and northern Great Basin | 26 | off | off | **24** |
| 7, Rockies | 24 | 37 | 31 | **24** |
| 10, northern and central Great Plains | 27 | 30 | 27 | **22** |
| 11, California annual grasslands | 17 | off | 21 | **14** |
| 12, southern Great Basin and Colorado Plateau | 38 | off | off | **37** |
| 13, upper Midwest | 19 | 19 | 19 | **16** |

: Curing error on held-out years by approach and region (bold: best, where it beats the typical date). "off": the fits gave no dates. The rules in each column are fitted per region on the same years. {.striped}

**Decision (October 12, replacing October 11).** Operational curing
uses **the typical date plus the weather adjustment** in every region except the southern
Plains and the mid-South, where **the soil-water bucket** (or GSI) does better; in the
monsoon Southwest the two tie. Green-up uses **the bucket** in the California annual
grasslands, the monsoon Southwest, the low deserts and the southern Plains, and **the
typical date** elsewhere. The model work on curing stops here. Before the write-up, the rule
is checked against the ground (below).

### Does the rule move curing dates toward the ground?

Everything above is scored against satellite dates. This check applies the rule at the NPN
grass sites' own cells, exactly as above (typical date from the fitting years, weather up to
14 days before, the coefficients fitted for the site's region and fold), and compares each
held-out year with the ground curing date (graminoid green falling below 50 %). Two
comparisons:

- **Difference from the ground**, in site-years where the typical date and the ground see the
  same season. This includes the satellite's average offset from the ground (about 20 days
  later for end of season), which the adjustment cannot change.
- **With each site's average offset removed**: does the adjustment move each year toward the
  ground's early or late year? The correlation of the adjustment with the ground's departure
  from its own average says the same thing directly.

The bucket rule for the southern Plains and the mid-South is not checked here; the ground
check of the satellite target found that in the mid-South the satellite does not follow the
ground's early and late years anyway.

```{r tab-curing-ground}
#| results: asis
f <- "figs/curing_adjust_ground_full.csv"
if (file.exists(f)) {
  tb <- utils::read.csv(f, check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  cat(knitr::kable(tb, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
                   caption = "Typical date and typical date plus adjustment against NPN grass curing (below 50 % green), held-out years, by region (regions with at least 3 sites)."), sep = "\n")
  cat("\n\n")
} else cat("*Results to come.*\n\n")
```

**Reading the ground check (October 13).**

- **Across CONUS the adjustment does not move curing dates toward the ground.** With each
  site's average offset removed, the typical date misses the ground's year-to-year swings by
  19.5 days and the adjusted date by 21.9; the adjustment correlates 0.08 with the ground's
  departures (674 site-years at 187 sites). The cured date gives the same answer.
- **Two regions are exceptions.** In the monsoon Southwest the adjustment follows the ground
  (correlation 0.43 for curing, 0.47 for the cured date) and cuts the error from 21.5 to 17.8
  days (cured: 17.1 to 15.3). In the California annual grasslands it follows the ground
  closely (0.66 and 0.83) and cuts the error from 5.3 to 4.2 days (cured: 6.0 to 3.2), but
  from only 10 site-years at 7 sites.
- **Where it gained most against the satellite it adds noise at the ground**: the Great
  Plains (19.4 to 25.4 days), the southern Plains (23.1 to 25.9), the upper Midwest (21.4
  to 25.8) and the mid-South (8.6 to 10.9).
- **Why.** At the same site-years the adjustment follows the satellite's departures
  (correlation 0.35), and the satellite follows the ground's only moderately (0.35 over all
  sites, about 0.55 in herbaceous cells; see the target check below). The part of the
  satellite signal the weather predicts is mostly not the part the grass sites share: in a
  4 km cell, end of season reflects the greenness of everything in it.
- **What that means.** A rule tuned to the satellite date should not be trusted for grass
  curing without a ground check. The ground supports the weather adjustment in the monsoon
  Southwest and, on few sites, the California annual grasslands. Elsewhere the typical date
  is the safer baseline. The bucket rule for the southern Plains and the mid-South has not
  been checked against the ground.

**Decision (October 13, amending October 12).** Curing uses **the typical date** as the
baseline everywhere, with **the weather adjustment** in the monsoon Southwest and, provisionally
(7 sites), the California annual grasslands, where the ground supports it. The bucket rules
(curing in the southern Plains and the mid-South; green-up in the California grasslands, the
monsoon Southwest, the low deserts and the southern Plains) are kept only if the ground check
below supports them; otherwise the typical date. After that the work turns to the write-up.

**The bucket rules at the ground.** The same check for the bucket rules (from the bucket test
above, fitted against the satellite dates), for curing and for green-up (graminoid green
rising through 50 %):

```{r tab-bucket-ground}
#| results: asis
for (nm in c("curing_bucket_ground", "greenup_bucket_ground")) {
  f <- sprintf("figs/%s_full.csv", nm)
  if (file.exists(f)) {
    tb <- utils::read.csv(f, check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
    cat(knitr::kable(tb, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
                     caption = if (grepl("greenup", nm)) "Typical green-up date and the bucket rule against NPN grass green-up (above 50 % green), held-out years, by region." else
                       "Typical curing date and the bucket rule against NPN grass curing (below 50 % green), held-out years, by region."), sep = "\n")
    cat("\n\n")
  } else if (nm == "curing_bucket_ground") cat("*Results to come.*\n\n")
}
```

**Reading the bucket check (October 13).** The bucket rules do not hold up at the ground
either. With each site's offset removed:

- **Curing**: in the southern Plains the bucket roughly doubles the error against the
  typical date (23 to 43 days; correlation 0.02), and in the mid-South it adds about 3 days
  (8.6 to 11.9). Across all sites, 19.5 to 28.3 days.
- **Green-up**: worse in the southern Plains (21 to 30 days) and the monsoon Southwest (23 to
  43), where in some years the bucket picks a different season. The California grasslands
  have no NPN green-up sites, and the low deserts three site-years, so the bucket's green-up
  gains there cannot be checked. The one region where it follows the ground is the Great
  Plains (correlation 0.42), where it barely changes the error (13.4 to 12.8 days).

**The rules, then.** Under the October 13 decision the bucket rules drop out, and what is left
is short:

| | Rule | Ground support |
|---|---|---|
| Curing, monsoon Southwest | Typical date plus weather adjustment (weather known 14 days ahead) | 30 sites: error 21.5 to 17.8 days, correlation 0.43 |
| Curing, California annual grasslands | Typical date plus weather adjustment, provisional | 7 sites: error 5.3 to 4.2 days, correlation 0.66 |
| Curing, everywhere else | Each cell's typical date | Every weather rule tried added error at the ground |
| Green-up, everywhere | Each cell's typical date | The bucket, the only rule to beat it against the satellite, did not at the ground |

: Per-region rules after the ground checks. The typical date is each cell's median satellite date (NDVI end of season for curing, NDVI green-up) over the available years. {.striped}

### The packaged rules and typical-date maps

The rules above are packaged as maps and a small model, built from the full record (scripts 40
and 41):

- **Typical dates.** For every 4 km cell, the median satellite green-up and curing date
  (NDVI end of season) over the record, their year-to-year spread (interquartile range), the
  strict herbaceous mask, the working region, and a flag for the cells where the curing
  adjustment applies (herbaceous cells in the monsoon Southwest and the California annual
  grasslands). Every land cell gets a date, so the product covers all of CONUS.
- **A confidence class per cell.** (1) Herbaceous cells in regions whose rule was checked
  against NPN grass sites (the southern Plains, the monsoon Southwest, the mid-South, the Great
  Plains, the California grasslands, the upper Midwest); (2) herbaceous cells in regions with
  few or no ground sites (the interior West, the low deserts, the Rockies); (3) mixed cover,
  outside the herbaceous mask, where the satellite date describes forest, crops and grass
  together rather than grass fuels.
- **The adjustment.** Its coefficients refitted on all years of the 4,000-cell sample, and
  each adjusted cell's own average of the cues it uses (so a year's cues become departures
  from that cell's normal).
- **A yearly run.** Given a year, and optionally an as-of date, the model reads daily PRISM up to
  each adjusted cell's cutoff (14 days before its typical curing date) and writes the expected
  curing date. Cells whose cutoff is still ahead keep the typical date. For a past year it also
  compares the result with that year's satellite date; the coefficients were fitted on all
  years, so that comparison is a consistency check, not a test.

```{r fig-rules-typical}
#| results: asis
show_fig("rules_typical",
  "Typical green-up and curing dates (median satellite dates) and their year-to-year spread, every land cell. Outlined on the curing map: the cells where the weather adjustment applies.",
  "Four maps of CONUS: typical green-up month, typical curing month, and the interquartile range of each across years.")
```

```{r fig-rules-confidence}
#| results: asis
show_fig("rules_confidence",
  "Confidence class of each cell's typical date: herbaceous cells in regions checked against NPN grass sites, herbaceous cells with few or no ground sites, and mixed cover, where the date describes forest and crops as well as grass.",
  "Map of CONUS in three classes of confidence in the typical date.")
```

**Reading the typical-date maps.** Every land cell has a date, but only the West and the
Plains are mostly herbaceous; east of the Plains the dates describe the greening and browning
of forest and cropland (green-up in April–May, end of season in October–November, into
December in the Southeast) and are marked as mixed cover, so read them as a landscape
calendar, not a grass-curing date. About a third of CONUS land cells are herbaceous; the
ground-checked class covers the Great Plains, the southern Plains, the monsoon Southwest and
the California grasslands, the few-sites class mostly the Great Basin and the low deserts. In the herbaceous West and Plains, green-up comes in December–February in the California grasslands and the low deserts,
in April–May across the Plains and the interior West, and with the summer rains (July–August)
in the monsoon Southwest and south Texas. Curing comes in May in California and the deserts,
June–July in the interior West, August–September on the northern Plains, and October–December
in the monsoon Southwest and Texas. The year-to-year spread is small (two to three weeks) for
green-up on the northern Plains and in the interior West, and largest (two to three months)
for both dates in the Southwest and south Texas, where the satellite season itself jumps
between years: there a single typical date is a weak guide.

**The adjustment as fitted on all years.** In the monsoon Southwest, more rain in the last 30
days delays curing (0.26 days per mm) and a later green-up delays it (0.16 days per day); the
cues explain 11 % of the year-to-year departures. In the California grasslands, a warmer last
two months brings curing earlier (2.6 days per degree), as does a long time since the last
soaking rain (0.13 days per day), and recent rain delays it (0.05 days per mm); 33 % explained.
In the example years the adjustment moves California's curing about two weeks earlier in dry
2021 and three or more weeks later after the wet winter of 2023. Against those years' satellite
dates it lowers California's error from 23.1 to 19.7 days (2021) and 14.4 to 9.6 days (2023),
and the monsoon Southwest's from 20.9 to 18.7 and 24.2 to 23.7 (consistency checks: the
coefficients were fitted on these years too).

```{r fig-rules-adjust}
#| results: asis
show_fig("rules_adjust",
  "The curing adjustment in two example years, in the cells where it applies: days earlier (red) or later (blue) than the typical curing date, from weather up to 14 days before it.",
  "Two maps of the western U.S. showing the curing adjustment in the monsoon Southwest and California for two years.")
```

**This year so far.** The yearly run is re-run as the season goes on, with daily PRISM up to
yesterday. Cells whose cutoff (14 days before the typical curing date) has passed show their
adjustment; the rest keep the typical date until their cutoff arrives. This year the
satellite green-up is not yet available, so the green-up cue counts as typical.

```{r fig-rules-current}
#| results: asis
show_fig("rules_current",
  "The curing adjustment for the current year, as of the date in the subtitle: cells whose cutoff has passed, in days from the typical curing date; dark grey, cells whose cutoff is still ahead.",
  "Map of the western U.S. showing this year's curing adjustment where its cutoff has passed.")
```

As of October 14, 2026, the adjustment puts California's curing (already past, in spring) 5 to
20 days earlier than typical, and the monsoon Southwest's 10 to 20 days later in Arizona and up
to a month later in northern New Mexico, after late-season rain. In southern New Mexico and
west Texas the cutoff is still ahead. These are the rule's estimates; they can be checked once
the 2026 satellite season is processed.

### Is the satellite curing date the right target?

The GSI tests above score the GSI against satellite dates: NDVI green-up and NDII7 curing.
If those dates are wrong in a region, the GSI could be blamed for the target's errors. So
the satellite dates were compared with ground observations of the same events at the same
places and in the same years: NPN grass green-up, curing (below 50 % green) and cured dates,
and herbaceous live fuel moisture decline dates. Dates are compared on a circular year, and a
difference of more than 90 days is counted as a *season mismatch* (for example, the satellite
picking the spring season and the ground the monsoon season).

| Ground event vs satellite date | Site-years | Median difference (satellite − ground) | Mean absolute difference | Within 30 days | Season mismatch | Year-to-year correlation (all cells / herbaceous cells) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Grass green-up vs NDVI green-up | 348 | −15 d | 42 d | 44 % | 9 % | 0.48 / 0.57 |
| Grass curing vs NDII7 curing | 632 | +14 d | 55 d | 48 % | 25 % | 0.27 / 0.55 |
| Grass curing vs NDVI end of season (50 %) | 645 | +17 d | 47 d | 51 % | 17 % | 0.35 / 0.56 |
| Grass cured vs NDII7 curing | 567 | −10 d | 51 d | 45 % | 20 % | 0.34 / 0.43 |
| Grass cured vs NDVI end of season (20 %) | 471 | +28 d | 49 d | 42 % | 16 % | 0.31 / 0.41 |
| Herbaceous fuel moisture decline vs NDII7 curing | 385 | −101 d | 109 d | 6 % | 71 % | 0.10 / 0.26 |

: Satellite season dates against ground observations, year by year (NPN grasses, one row per site and year, the median over a site's plants; Globe-LFMC herbaceous series). The year-to-year correlation compares each site's departures from its own average date, ground and satellite each measured from their own site median, in the site-years where satellite and ground see the same season (difference of 90 days or less), at sites with at least three such years. Herbaceous cells: sites in the strict herbaceous mask. Revised October 13, see below. {.striped}

| Region (13 regions) | Grass sites | NDII7 curing: within 30 days / season mismatch / correlation | NDVI end of season: within 30 days / season mismatch / correlation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1, Gulf and south Atlantic coastal plain | 26 | 44 % / 21 % / −0.21 | 44 % / 20 % / −0.14 |
| 2, southern Plains | 17 | 54 % / 11 % / 0.65 | 53 % / 15 % / 0.62 |
| 3, monsoon Southwest | 30 | 30 % / 49 % / 0.55 | 42 % / 26 % / 0.65 |
| 5, mid-South (with the tallgrass prairie) | 25 | 70 % / 11 % / 0.27 | 72 % / 10 % / 0.21 |
| 6, Snake River Plain and northern Great Basin | 6 | 0 % / 96 % / – | 0 % / 78 % / – |
| 10, northern and central Great Plains | 23 | 48 % / 36 % / 0.49 | 52 % / 16 % / 0.55 |
| 11, California annual grasslands | 7 | 64 % / 7 % / 0.77 | 77 % / 0 % / 0.48 |
| 12, southern Great Basin and Colorado Plateau | 4 | 6 % / 61 % / – | 39 % / 11 % / 0.71 |
| 13, upper Midwest | 27 | 53 % / 10 % / 0.61 | 44 % / 12 % / 0.31 |

: Grass curing (below 50 % green) against the satellite curing and end-of-season dates by region, year by year. "–": too few site-years without a season mismatch. The low deserts have two grass sites and are left out. {.striped}

**Reading the target check.**

- **The satellite curing date follows the ground's early and late years moderately, and
  only in grassland cells.** Where both see the same season, the correlation is about 0.55
  at sites in herbaceous cells, but 0.27–0.35 over all sites, because sites in mixed cells
  (the Gulf coastal plain most of all) do not follow at all. By region it is 0.5–0.65 in the
  southern Plains, the monsoon Southwest and the Great Plains, and about 0.2 in the mid-South.
- **Corrections (October 12–13).** The first version of this table counted each NPN plant as
  a site-year (several plants of a species are often observed at one site), and built the
  satellite's departure from the ground date plus the difference, which copied ground
  outliers (for example a February "curing" at a site that cures in the fall) into the
  satellite. Both inflated the year-to-year correlation (first reported as 0.70–0.77).
  Dates on either side of January 1 are also handled on a circular year now.
- **Average timing and season matching are the weak points of the target.** The satellite
  date is often a month or more from the ground date, and a sixth to a quarter of site-years
  pick a different season. NDVI end of season matches the ground's timing better than NDII7
  curing, with fewer season mismatches, most of all in the monsoon Southwest (26 against
  49 %) and the Great Plains (16 against 36 %).
- **In the California grasslands and the mid-South the target's timing is good**: 64–77 % of
  site-years within 30 days and few mismatches. In the mid-South, though, the satellite
  follows the ground's early and late years only weakly: ground curing there varies little
  from year to year, and what varies is not what the satellite sees.
- **In the monsoon Southwest the target is part of the problem.** A quarter to half of
  site-years pick a different season from the ground.
- **At the six Snake River Plain sites the satellite date is about four months later than
  the ground** (78–96 % mismatches): it does not describe these grass sites, which may be in
  towns or irrigated land.
- **Live fuel moisture decline dates are a different event.** They come 3–4 months before the
  satellite curing date (71 % mismatches), so they cannot check it.
- **Caveats.** Ground sites are points; the satellite date describes a 4 km cell that often
  mixes grass with other cover. Several regions have few sites, and the low deserts have
  almost none.

```{r fig-obs-sites}
#| results: asis
show_fig("obs_sites",
  "Where the ground observations are. NPN grass observations (the most direct check on herbaceous green-up and curing) are sparse; live fuel moisture sites are mostly western and woody.",
  "Map of CONUS with points for iNaturalist, NPN, live fuel moisture and NPN grass observation sites.")
```

### Fitting to the ground: the NPN curing study (first result)

The ground checks above showed that rules tuned to satellite dates rarely carry over to NPN
grass sites. The NPN curing study asks the question directly on the ground observations:
can weather explain a grass's early and late years at its own site?

**Methods.**

- **Unit.** One series-year per site, species and year, the median over that site-year's
  observed plants, from plants with at least 12 readings. Green-up and curing are the dates
  the plant passes 50 % green going up and coming down; the cured date is when it is fully
  cured. Crops (wheat, corn) are left out, and species are labeled C3 (cool-season) or C4
  (warm-season) from the literature.
- **Record.** 707 series-years in 181 series (86 sites, 67 species), 2014–2024. A series
  needs at least 3 years with the date to be scored: 289 green-up, 529 curing and 461 cured
  series-years. Dates more than 90 days from the series' usual date (2–4 %) count as a
  season mismatch and are not scored.
- **Weather.** Daily PRISM at each site, 2001–2025: growing degree-days, seasonal
  temperature, freeze dates, chilling, seasonal rain, vapour pressure deficit, rain events
  and dry spells, monsoon onset, and a moisture memory (a running average of daily
  precipitation minus potential evapotranspiration, over 15, 30 and 60 days). Each is used
  as a departure from the site's own average, so place is removed from both sides.
- **Two sets of curing drivers.** *Lead*: only weather known by the series' typical date
  minus 14 days (spring conditions, rain after the typical green-up, moisture memory and
  heat at that cutoff), the operational case. *Hindcast*: adds the summer and fall windows,
  which can run past the date.
- **The ladder**, the same data, folds and scores at each step:
  - **L0, typical date:** the series' average over the training years. This is the bar.
  - **L1, one driver:** March–April temperature for green-up; moisture memory at the cutoff
    (lead) or June–August rain (hindcast) for curing.
  - **L2, process rule:** green-up when growing degree-days reach the series' usual amount;
    curing when the 30-day moisture memory falls below the series' usual level and stays
    there (within 60 days of the typical date), or at the first hard fall freeze if earlier.
  - **L3, regression:** up to four drivers chosen by forward selection, per C3/C4.
  - **L4, random forest:** all drivers plus site climate, pathway and life cycle.
- **Scoring.** Leave one year out (every series loses the same year at once). Mean absolute
  error in days; skill = 1 − error / error of the typical date; and the correlation of each
  model's predicted departure with the observed one.

**Results.**

| Date | Series-years | Typical-date error | L1 | L2 | L3 | L4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Green-up | 289 | 24.8 days | 0.00 | −0.04 | −0.02 | −0.02 |
| 50 % curing | 529 | 27.6 days | 0.00 | −0.33 | −0.04 | −0.02 |
| Cured | 461 | 23.7 days | +0.01 | −0.17 | −0.05 | −0.03 |

: Skill against the typical date (0 = no better, negative = worse), lead driver set {.striped}

- **No step beats the typical date.** The best is one driver for the cured date (+0.01,
  correlation 0.15). The process rules, the regression and the random forest all add
  error. The same holds for C3 and C4 separately, in each region with enough data, when
  species are averaged within a site-year, and with the hindcast drivers that can see
  past the date.
- **The regression does not settle on drivers.** Its choices change from one left-out
  year to the next.
- **The ceiling is low.** Species observed at the same site in the same year share only
  part of their early or late year: 22 % of the year-to-year variance for green-up, 24 %
  for curing and 40 % for the cured date. The rest is specific to the plant or the
  observer, which no weather record can explain.

**How much of the year-to-year variation could weather explain? (variance partition)**

To measure the ceiling directly, each plant's date is split into parts with a mixed model
on all plant-years (5,780 plant-years, 1,514 plants, 84 sites; plant dates more than 90 days
from the series' usual date, 5–10 %, are left out): place (site, species, and
the species at that site), a year signal shared by the grasses at a site (national,
regional and site-wide), a year signal of one species at one site, and what is left for
the single plant.

| Date | Plant-years | Place, % of all variation | Year-to-year SD | Shared by the site's grasses | Region-wide part of that | One species only | Single plant |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Green-up | 2,563 | 68 % | 30 days | 39 % | 28 % | 23 % | 39 % |
| 50 % curing | 4,468 | 72 % | 35 days | 26 % | 10 % | 21 % | 53 % |
| Cured | 3,225 | 80 % | 30 days | 38 % | 3 % | 22 % | 39 % |

: Variance partition of NPN grass dates; the last four columns are shares of the year-to-year variation {.striped}

- **Place dominates.** Two-thirds to four-fifths of the variation in a plant's date is where
  it grows and what species it is. That is what the typical-date maps carry.
