- **Of the year-to-year part, a quarter to two-fifths is shared** by the grasses at a site:
  about 18 days (standard deviation) for each date. That shared part is the most any
  weather record at the site could explain, and the ladder above explained almost none of
  it. So the ceiling is real but not zero: the weather drivers tried so far miss a
  shared signal that exists.
- **Green-up moves together across a region** (28 % of its year-to-year variation);
  curing and the cured date mostly do not (10 % and 3 %). Their shared signal is local to
  the site. Local weather is one explanation; so are things that act on a whole site in a
  year, such as mowing, grazing, irrigation or a change of observer, which the data cannot
  separate.
- **Half of the year-to-year variation in 50 % curing belongs to the single plant**,
  more for warm-season (C4) grasses (62 %) than cool-season (C3, 36 %). The spacing of
  readings accounts for only 1–3 % of it, so it is not a sampling artefact: plants of one
  species at one site really differ (microsite, age, how each observer judges "percent
  green").
- **Averaging the plants helps but does not remove it.** In a site-species-year mean
  (median 3–5 plants) the shared part is about half (45–55 %) of the year-to-year variation.

**Does the shared signal follow local weather?** The shared part was estimated for each
site-year from the same model (203–290 site-years at 64–71 sites) and compared with that
year's weather departures at the site.

- **For curing and the cured date it does, weakly, and in the expected direction.** Within
  a year, sites with a wetter spring, more summer rain events or lower summer vapour
  pressure deficit cure later (correlations 0.2–0.27; strongest: June–August VPD, April–June
  rain, April–September rain events, and VPD in the 30 days before the typical date).
- **But not enough to predict it.** Fitted on the other years, the best single driver
  explains 3–4 % of the shared signal in a left-out year, and a selected set of drivers
  explains none. So most of the site-wide year signal is something the 4 km weather record
  does not see: very local weather and soil, or what happens at the site (mowing, grazing,
  irrigation, a new observer).
- **Managed sites are not the explanation.** Gardens, yards, campuses and parks are only
  about 4 % of the usable plant-years, too few to fit on their own; the results without them
  are unchanged.
- **The record is mostly NEON.** 96 % of the usable plant-years come from the 36 National
  Ecological Observatory Network field sites, where trained technicians follow five tagged
  plants per species in natural plots. Results without NEON sites are too thin to compare
  (124–154 plant-years). So the large plant share is not volunteer noise: it is real
  plant-to-plant variation within a plot plus how each technician judges "percent green",
  and the site-wide year signal may include crew changes and visit schedules as well as
  weather.
- **For green-up, the links are with summer temperature, after the event,** so they reflect
  which years were warm overall rather than a cause, and they do not carry over to a
  left-out year either.

**What it means.** On the ground, as with the satellite rules checked above, the typical
date is the baseline to beat, and so far nothing beats it. There is a shared year signal of
about 18 days, regional for green-up and local for curing, that the weather drivers tried
here capture only weakly (moisture and VPD, in the expected direction). An independent,
observer-free check is available at the same NEON sites: PhenoCam cameras photograph the
plots daily. If the camera's grass greenness shows the same early and late years, the
site-wide signal is real vegetation; if not, it is mostly how the plants were observed.
That check, and the record and dates by region and grass type, are the next steps.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Reading the first comparisons
- **Climate regions capture seasonal timing better than location alone.** On the
  timing-only curves in herbaceous cells, A1 explains 50, 54 and 58 % of the variance at
  7, 10 and 13 regions, against 36, 45 and 47 % for compact blobs of the same number.
- **Adding Block 2 (A2) does not improve the national scores.** A1 and A2 are tied on
  timing (A2: 49, 53, 55 %), and A1 is ahead on the curves as observed in herbaceous
  cells (40 vs 29 % at 7 regions, 53 vs 50 % at 13). Against the ground observations, the
  A2-minus-A1 range spans zero for every data set. Block 2's gains are local: at 13
  regions A2 separates the Kansas and Oklahoma tallgrass prairie from the eastern Corn
  Belt and the California annual grasslands from the Mojave.
- **The level + shape satellite regions mostly sort cells by how green they get.** They
  explain the curves best (they are fitted to them) but separate the ground dates poorly.
- **Where the ground data can judge, climate wins.** Climate regions clearly beat location
  alone for the woody live fuel moisture peak (about +0.12 to +0.21 in adjusted
  R-squared), iNaturalist flowering (+0.05) and grass cured dates at 7 regions (+0.25).
  Grass green-up beats location only at 13 regions. At 10 to 13 regions location alone
  does as well on grass curing and cured dates: with about 150 to 190 grass sites,
  clustered in a few places, the observations cannot judge finer regions.
- **NPN leaf onset and end** for herbaceous and woody plants barely separate by any set of
  regions (adjusted R-squared under 0.07) and are likely too noisy as site medians.
- **Number of regions:** about 13 regions describes herbaceous timing best, but several of
  those regions have fewer than five grass sites and no herbaceous fuel moisture sites,
  so fitting phenology models in every region is not yet possible. About 7 regions, the
  most stable level of A2, is what today's observations can support. This led to the
  decision to use 13 regions nested into 7 (below).
:::

## What the candidate regions look like

Scores say how well a set of regions works on average; profiles say what the regions
are. For each candidate set, the tabs below show a numbered map, the median climate and
satellite-season values of every region, the satellite seasonal curves, and the ground
observation dates that fall in each region. Region numbers and colours are the same in
the map, table and charts of a tab, and a region keeps its colour from tab to tab where it
covers mostly the same area. Season dates and curves come from the strict herbaceous cells
of a region when it has at least 200 of them, otherwise from all of its cells.

```{r profiles-setup}
#| include: false
show_prof_table <- function(id, caption) {
  f <- NULL
  for (pr in c("full", "dev")) {
    g <- sprintf("figs/prof_table_%s_%s.csv", id, pr)
    if (file.exists(g)) { f <- g; break }
  }
  if (is.null(f)) return(invisible())
  t <- utils::read.csv(f, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, check.names = FALSE)
  cat(knitr::kable(t, align = c("r", rep("r", ncol(t) - 2), "l"), caption = caption), sep = "\n")
  cat("\n\n")
}
show_crosswalk <- function(fine, coarse, caption) {
  f <- NULL
  for (pr in c("full", "dev")) {
    g <- sprintf("figs/prof_crosswalk_%s__%s_%s.csv", fine, coarse, pr)
    if (file.exists(g)) { f <- g; break }
  }
  if (is.null(f)) return(invisible())
  cw <- utils::read.csv(f)
  cw <- cw[cw$share_of_fine >= 0.05, ]
  out <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(cw, cw$fine), function(d) {
    d <- d[order(-d$share_of_fine), ]
    data.frame(`Fine region` = d$fine[1],
               `Coarse region (share of cells)` = paste(sprintf("%d (%.0f%%)", d$coarse, 100 * d$share_of_fine), collapse = ", "),
               check.names = FALSE)
  }))
  cat(knitr::kable(out, row.names = FALSE, caption = caption), sep = "\n")
  cat("\n\n")
}
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Climate A2, 13 regions

```{r prof-a2-13}
#| results: asis
show_fig("prof_map_A2_groups_k13", "Climate A2 at 13 regions.", "Map of CONUS with 13 numbered climate regions.")
show_prof_table("A2_groups_k13", "Climate A2, 13 regions: median climate and satellite season by region")
show_fig("prof_heat_A2_groups_k13", "Region medians of the climate features and satellite season metrics (all cells), coloured by how far each region is above or below the average across regions.", "Heatmap of features by region with median values.")
show_fig("prof_curves_A2_groups_k13", "Median NDVI and NDII7 seasonal curves per region, with the range of the middle half of the cells.", "Thirteen small charts of seasonal NDVI and NDII7 curves, one per region.")
show_fig("prof_obs_A2_groups_k13", "Ground observation dates by region: each dot is one site (median date across years).", "Six dot plots of observed phenology dates by region.")
show_crosswalk("A2_groups_k13", "A2_groups_k07", "How the 13 regions fit into the 7 (regions holding at least 5 % of a fine region's cells)")
```

**Reading the 13 regions.** In the West and Plains the regions line up with recognizable
herbaceous fuel types, each with its own season:

- **3, monsoon Southwest** (southern Arizona and New Mexico, west Texas; Santa Rita,
  Sevilleta, Chino Valley): nearly half the precipitation falls in July–September, the
  warm-season rains start around July 1, and grasses green up in early June and peak in
  late August.
- **2, southern Plains** (central and south Texas, western Oklahoma): green-up around
  April 1, a broad peak from late June into the fall, and the most variable rainfall
  outside the deserts.
- **11, California annual grasslands** (Sierra Foothills): over half the precipitation in
  January–March and none in summer; green-up comes with the fall rains (median early
  December), peak in late March, curing in late May.
- **4, low deserts** (Mojave and lower Colorado River): little rain, no regular
  warm-season onset, a small green flush in February–March and curing in early May.
- **6 and 12, the interior West** (Snake River Plain and northern Great Basin; southern
  Great Basin and Colorado Plateau): spring green-up, peak in late May and curing in June.
  They differ more in how much they green up than in when.
- **10, northern and central Great Plains** (CPER, Cheyenne): green-up in early April,
  peak in mid June, curing in early August.
- **7, the Rockies** and **9, the Pacific Northwest**: cold or wet mountain and coastal
  regions with summer curing.

In the East the regions follow climate gradients across land that is mostly forest and
cropland: **1** (Gulf and south Atlantic coastal plain), **5** (mid-South, which also takes
in the Kansas and Oklahoma tallgrass prairie), **8** (Midwest and Northeast, with almost no
strict herbaceous cells) and **13** (upper Midwest). Their season curves describe the
mixed land cover more than grasses.

### Climate A2, 7 regions

```{r prof-a2-7}
#| results: asis
show_fig("prof_map_A2_groups_k07", "Climate A2 at 7 regions.", "Map of CONUS with 7 numbered climate regions.")
show_prof_table("A2_groups_k07", "Climate A2, 7 regions: median climate and satellite season by region")
show_fig("prof_heat_A2_groups_k07", "Region medians of the climate features and satellite season metrics (all cells).", "Heatmap of features by region with median values.")
show_fig("prof_curves_A2_groups_k07", "Median NDVI and NDII7 seasonal curves per region.", "Seven small charts of seasonal NDVI and NDII7 curves, one per region.")
show_fig("prof_obs_A2_groups_k07", "Ground observation dates by region.", "Six dot plots of observed phenology dates by region.")
```

**Reading the 7 regions.** The seven are broad and very stable, but three of them pool
herbaceous fuels with different calendars:

- **2** joins the monsoon Southwest with the southern Plains. Its median green-up (late
  April) and peak (late August) fall between two quite different seasons: an early-April
  green-up in the southern Plains and an early-June green-up with the monsoon.
- **3** joins the California annual grasslands with the low deserts: a fall-to-spring
  season in both, but the California grasslands green up two months earlier and have about
  four times the greenness amplitude.
- **7** joins the northern Plains with the upper Midwest, where curing comes about two
  months later (early October against early August).

The other four (Southeast, interior West, Rockies and Pacific Northwest, Midwest and
Northeast) are about as uniform in season timing as their parts at 13 regions.

### Climate A1, 10 regions

```{r prof-a1-10}
#| results: asis
show_fig("prof_map_A1_groups_k10", "Climate A1 (Block 1 only) at 10 regions, the working set from October 7 to 9.", "Map of CONUS with 10 numbered climate regions.")
show_prof_table("A1_groups_k10", "Climate A1, 10 regions: median climate and satellite season by region")
show_fig("prof_heat_A1_groups_k10", "Region medians of the climate features and satellite season metrics (all cells).", "Heatmap of features by region with median values.")
show_fig("prof_curves_A1_groups_k10", "Median NDVI and NDII7 seasonal curves per region.", "Ten small charts of seasonal NDVI and NDII7 curves, one per region.")
show_fig("prof_obs_A1_groups_k10", "Ground observation dates by region.", "Six dot plots of observed phenology dates by region.")
```

**Reading the 10 regions.** A1 already separates the monsoon Southwest (3) from the
southern Plains (2). Its two weak spots for herbaceous fuels are the California annual
grasslands, which it splits between region 9 (Sierra foothills, with the wet Pacific
Northwest) and region 4 (Central Valley and southern California, with the low deserts),
and the tallgrass prairie, which shares region 5 with the Ohio Valley. A2 at 13 regions
gives the California grasslands their own region and moves the tallgrass prairie out of
the Ohio Valley region.

### A2 herbaceous-weighted, 13 regions

```{r prof-a2h-13}
#| results: asis
show_fig("prof_map_A2_herbw_k13", "Climate A2 at 13 regions with cells weighted by open herbaceous cover, so grass- and shrub-dominated land counts more in shaping the regions.", "Map of CONUS with 13 numbered climate regions, herbaceous-weighted.")
show_prof_table("A2_herbw_k13", "Climate A2, herbaceous-weighted, 13 regions: median climate and satellite season by region")
show_fig("prof_heat_A2_herbw_k13", "Region medians of the climate features and satellite season metrics (all cells).", "Heatmap of features by region with median values.")
show_fig("prof_curves_A2_herbw_k13", "Median NDVI and NDII7 seasonal curves per region.", "Thirteen small charts of seasonal NDVI and NDII7 curves, one per region.")
show_fig("prof_obs_A2_herbw_k13", "Ground observation dates by region.", "Six dot plots of observed phenology dates by region.")
show_crosswalk("A2_herbw_k13", "A2_groups_k13", "How the herbaceous-weighted regions relate to the unweighted 13 (regions holding at least 5 % of a weighted region's cells)")
```

**Reading the herbaceous-weighted 13.** Weighting by herbaceous cover moves regions from
the East to the West, as intended. Compared with the unweighted 13:

- **The Southwest gets more detail.** The monsoon region splits into a core monsoon region
  (**11**: southeastern Arizona and southwestern New Mexico, with Santa Rita, Sevilleta and
  Chino Valley; half the precipitation in July–September, green-up in late June, peak in
  early September) and a fringe to the north and east (**3**: green-up in late April, peak
  in late August). The interior West splits three ways (**5**, **6**, **12**), separating
  the cooler basins that cure in early July from the drier ones that cure by mid June.
- **California and the low deserts keep their own regions** (**13** and **4**), as in the
  unweighted 13.
- **The East loses detail.** It falls into two broad regions (**1**, the Southeast, and
  **8**, the Midwest and Northeast). The Kansas tallgrass prairie goes back in with the Ohio
  Valley (region 8), the Oklahoma tallgrass joins the Southeast, and the upper Midwest is
  split between region 8 and the northern Plains (**10**).

On the scores, the weighted regions explain seasonal timing in the herbaceous cells about
as well as A1 and slightly better than unweighted A2 (timing-only curves: 0.51, 0.54 and
0.59 at 7, 10 and 13 regions, against 0.49, 0.53 and 0.55 for unweighted A2). Against the ground data they are indistinguishable
from unweighted A2, except a lower score on the herbaceous live fuel moisture peak at 10
and 13 regions, which rests on only 115 sites. Like unweighted A2, they are most stable at
7 regions.

:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## What the profiles suggest for the number of regions
Going from 7 to 13 regions pays off for herbaceous fuels in three splits: monsoon
Southwest from southern Plains, California grasslands from low deserts, and northern Plains
from upper Midwest. Each separates seasons that differ by one to two months. The other
splits divide the interior West by how much it greens up, or divide the East where
herbaceous cells are few. That points to a working set between the two (about 10 regions
with those three splits), or to 13 regions that are rolled up to fewer for fitting models.
Ground data are thin at 13 regions: six regions have five or fewer NPN grass green-up
sites, and four have no herbaceous live fuel moisture sites.

**Decision (October 9).** The working regions are **A2 at 13 regions**, nested into A2 at
7 regions. None of the tests separate 7 from 13 on skill (the satellite curves, the ground
observations and the GSI model test are all within noise), so the choice rests on what the
regions describe: 13 keeps the three western splits that separate seasons by one to two
months. Models are fitted at 13 where a region has enough data and at 7 where it does not.
The herbaceous-weighted 13 regions stay as a sensitivity check for western fuels: they
add western detail but lose the tallgrass and upper Midwest splits.
:::

{{< include _worked_examples.qmd >}}

## Clustering and evaluation plan

Methods will be judged by how well the regions work as domains for regional phenology
models, not by clustering scores alone.

- **Cut A (done for A1, A2, A3):** k-means as the baseline, Gaussian mixtures and Ward
  hierarchical clustering (nested regions: fine for modeling, coarse for operational
  roll-up). The Gaussian mixtures are overconfident so far (almost every cell gets a
  membership near 1) and need retuning before they can map transition zones.
  **Still to do:** a spatially constrained version, to test how much is lost by requiring
  contiguous regions.
- **Cut B (done):** principal components of the seasonal curves (on smooth, regularly
  spaced curves this is functional PCA), then k-means, for the curves as observed and for
  timing only.
- **Evaluation (done):** stability under spatial resampling; agreement between partitions;
  share of the satellite curves explained; ground observations with block-bootstrap
  ranges; year-to-year synchrony; and the GSI fitted per region.
  **Still to do:** stability under resampling of years, and comparison with EPA ecoregions
  and operational units (Predictive Service Areas, NFDRS climate classes).
- **Phenology rules (done):** GSI forms, a soil-water bucket and a weather adjustment of
  the typical date, each fitted per region against satellite dates and checked against
  NPN grass sites (see the four steps under [How the analysis is built](#how-the-analysis-is-built)).
- **Still to do, linking A and B:** cluster the curves, then predict those regions from
  the climate features with random forests. This gives a wall-to-wall map and shows which
  climate features separate phenology regions.

## Decisions so far

| Date | Decision | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Oct 2026 | Start with herbaceous fuels; regions are domains for regional phenology models | Most direct need raised by fire managers; herbaceous fuels respond fastest |
| Oct 2026 | Build Cut A from daily PRISM at 4 km; features per year, then summarized | Daily data capture timing and variability; averaging climate first distorts nonlinear indices like GSI |
| Oct 2026 | Herbaceous cover from Annual NLCD (grassland + shrub/scrub; 2001, 2012, 2024) | Consistent national product; combined share avoids the state-line artifact |
| Oct 2026 | Regions are wall to wall across CONUS | Lets NPN and iNaturalist observations anywhere test the regions; cover is an attribute, not the domain |
| Oct 2026 | Cut B from MODIS MOD13A2 + MYD13A2 (1 km, 16-day), averaged to 4 km; NDVI and NDII7 | Available nationally through AppEEARS; two sensors double the sampling; NDII7 tracks curing |
| Oct 2026 | Data period starts in 2001 | First full year of MODIS, so the climate and satellite cuts overlap |
| Oct 2026 | Block 1 definitions: water year, Oct–Dec/Jan–Mar/Apr–Jun/Jul–Sep seasons, GDD base 5 and 10 °C, freeze at 0 °C (−2.2 °C sensitivity), Hargreaves aridity | Seasons isolate the monsoon and the dry foresummer; bases fit cool- and warm-season grasses |
| Oct 2026 | Soils deferred | No quick national water-holding capacity layer; add if the first runs suggest it matters |
| Oct 2026 | Block 2 definitions: rain event ≥ 5 mm (2.5 and 10 mm sensitivity), dry day < 1 mm, warm-season onset rule (10-day total ≥ 20 mm from May 1, no 20-day dry spell in the next 30), hard freeze ≤ −2.2 °C | Event size that wets the root zone of grasses; onset rule screens out false starts |
| Oct 2026 | Feature groups weighted equally within a block (temperature, moisture amount, seasonality) | With one group, temperature features dominated and the Plains moisture gradient was lost |
| Oct 2026 | GSI variants: national literature and FEMS operational parameters; no moisture, 28-day precipitation or KBDI; with and without VPD; GSI Scout's model code reused | Tests how far local tuning has drifted from the national default, and which moisture control matters where |
| Oct 7 2026 | Working climate regions: A1 at 10 regions, pending the comparison with satellite curves and ground observations (replaced Oct 9) | Stable, and separates the main grassland types |
| Oct 9 2026 | **Working regions: A2 at 13 regions, nested into A2 at 7** for fitting where data are thin; herbaceous-weighted 13 as a western sensitivity check | Skill is flat between 7 and 13; 13 keeps three western splits (monsoon Southwest vs southern Plains, California grasslands vs low deserts, northern Plains vs upper Midwest) |
| Oct 9 2026 | A3 = A2 + GSI features (FEMS operational settings with the 28-day precipitation ramp; without VPD and with KBDI as sensitivity runs) | Tests whether the GSI as run today adds to, or steers, the regions |
| Oct 10 2026 | A2 stays the working set after A3: the GSI features add little to the regions and make them less stable | A3 vs A2 within noise on satellite timing, ground observations and synchrony; stability 0.74 against 0.83 at 7 regions |
| Oct 11 2026 | Curing baseline (under revision October 12: the region names came from mislabeled tables): each place's typical curing date in the monsoon Southwest, mid-South, southern Plains and California annual grasslands; GSI or soil-water bucket where they beat it (Great Plains, Snake River Plain); bucket for green-up | No model tried beats the typical curing date in those four regions, with either satellite target; region-specific rules are screened next |
| Oct 12 2026 | **Curing and green-up rules** (replacing October 11): curing = typical date plus a weather adjustment from weather known 14 days ahead, except the soil-water bucket in the southern Plains and the mid-South; green-up = bucket in the California grasslands, monsoon Southwest, low deserts and southern Plains, typical date elsewhere | The adjustment beats the typical date in every region and is best in 8 of 10; the bucket is better in the two regions where it beats both. Curing model work stops; the rule is checked against the ground before the write-up |
| Oct 13 2026 | **Curing rules amended after the ground check:** typical date everywhere, weather adjustment in the monsoon Southwest and (provisionally) the California annual grasslands; bucket rules kept only where the ground check supports them; then the write-up | The adjustment improved the satellite fit everywhere but added error at the ground except in those two regions: rules tuned to the satellite need a ground check |

: Analysis decisions {.striped}

## Open questions for the team

- **Study period:** use all of 2001–2025, or a fixed recent window?
- **Curing rules:** the typical date everywhere, with a weather adjustment in the monsoon
  Southwest and California. Is a few days' gain there worth a second method for managers,
  and is a 14-day lead the right operational case? Models fitted to the NPN ground dates
  directly (October 16) did not beat the typical date either; is the typical date, with a
  clear statement of its spread, the right product for now?
- **Ground observations:** which NPN and iNaturalist taxa and phenophases best
  represent herbaceous fuel green-up and curing?
- **Operational use:** how contiguous do regions need to be to be useful to managers?
- **C3/C4 grasses:** is there a suitable national layer of cool- versus warm-season
  grass cover?

Comments on any of these are welcome.
